newsitem.title: GERMANY: Complaint filed with EU against Deutsche Telekom.
newsitem.headline: Complaint filed with EU against Deutsche Telekom.

text.p: A would-be competitor to Deutsche Telekom AG said on Tuesday it had filed a complaint with the European Commission against the communications giant for using its position as a monopoly to stifle competition.

Telit Deutschland GmbH, a distributor of telecommunications services, said the complaint was filed last week with the offices of European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert and urged the EU to strip Telekom of its fixed-wire network.
"The entire public network should be separated from Deutsche Telekom so that the company is a service provider just like its competitors," Telit managing director Berthold Stauffenberg told Reuters.

Stauffenberg said the benefits to new telecommunications companies would be that in future they would negotiate over leasing lines for services with an independent company instead of their main competitor and the most dominant market player.

He said Telit became frustrated earlier this year after it tried and failed to reach an agreement with Deutsche Telekom over access to its public network to offer communications services to third parties.
"The costs of access would have been so high that the business would not have been profitable," he said.

Industry sources said they did not expect the complaint had much chance of winning. But it makes an issue public that has long frustrated competitors just as Telekom is preparing to launch a 15-billion-mark ($10-billion) listing on stock exchanges.
Deutsche Telekom could not confirm that the complaint had been filed, but a spokesman said: "If it has been filed, we wouldn't be too bothered about it."
The German post and telecommunications ministry was unaware of the complaint. It is also indirectly a target as the complaint was also directed against the German government.
Competitors to Telekom have argued that unless they are given inexpensive access to the company's extensive public network, they will not be able to compete on equal terms.
The European Commission is preparing a study on the effects on competition of monopoly fixed-wire networks when European telecommunications markets are liberalised in 1998.
"Because of this study, we think we have a good chance of winning," said Stauffenberg.
